Bodhyagītā
(‘that [which is] sung [by the sage] Bodhya’)
------------------------------------------
The extreme popularity and importance of the Bhagavadgītā gave rise, in course of time, to a number of religio-philosophical tracts of varying lengths composed in verse form to which the title ‘Gītā’ was appended. The Mahābhārata alone contains sixteen of them, and the Bodhyagītā is one such.
It is a short piece of only ten verses (Śāntiparva 17

) and contains the teaching given by the sage Bodhya to the king ययाति.
The sage declares that he learnt great lessons in his life by observing the following persons and animals during the course of his wanderings as a mendicant: a prostitute called पिङ्गला, the bird kurara or osprey, a serpent, the legendary cātaka bird (Cucculus melanolecucus) that lives on rain drops, a blacksmith who prepared arrows and an unmarried girl.
From Pīṅgalā he learnt the spirit of renunciation; from the osprey, that attachment leads to misery; from the serpent that one should be homeless; from the cātaka bird that one should live on alms without being a burden to anyone; from the blacksmith, concentration of मिन्द्; and, from the unmarried girl, that one should live all alone to avoid quarrels and misunderstandings.
This Gītā seems to be a summary of the story of the अवधूत with 24 teachers in the Bhāgavata (11.7-9).

bodhana
(‘awakening’)
------------------------------------------
Durgāpūjā, worship of the Divine मोथेर् दुर्गा, celebrated for nine days or for three days, during the month of Āśvayuja or Āśvina (September/October), is a major festival of the Hindus.
According to Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्, the various gods and goddesses go to sleep for a period of four months (from आषाढ to Kārttīka, July to October). Since the दुर्गापूजा is celebrated in the month of Āśvina when दुर्गा is still asleep, she has to be woken up first. This ceremonial waking up of the deity is called ‘bodhana.’ It is done on the evening of Āśvina śukla षष्ठी, (sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina). A घट or कलश (a pot with water containing sandalwood paste, दूर्वा grass, leaves of five trees like mango, clay from seven places, fruit etc.) is established under a बिल्व tree (Aegle marmelos), the mantras of बोधन or awakening are uttered, and the बिल्व tree itself is worshipped as the मोथेर् दुर्गा.
The story goes that when दुर्गा (Pārvatī, the spouse of शिव) came to her मोथेर्’s होउसे from her husband’s home, it was late in the evening. So, she decided not to disturb her parents and spent the whole night under a बिल्व tree near the होउसे. The ritual described above, is symbolic of this.
Bodhana is also one of the ten aspects of a ritual aimed at making a मन्त्र (divine formula) potent. See MANTRA-SAṀSKĀRA for details.

Bodhāyana
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta-दर्शन, one of the six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, is based mainly on the Brahmasūtras, which again, is a work that systematizes the philosophical ideas occurring in the उपनिषद्स्.
Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) wrote an admirable commentary—the Śrībhāṣya—on the Brahmasūtras according to the Viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy and Vaiṣṇava religion. He is said to have acquired a copy of the Vṛtti (gloss) on the Brahma-sūtras written by an ancient teacher बोधायन, which was quite voluminous and which he (Rāmānuja) had faithfully followed while composing the Śrībhāṣya. Who this बोधायन was, is not known; nor is his work available. He is sometimes identified with उपवर्ष (also called वृत्तिकार), who again, had been known as Kṛtakoṭi and Halabhūti also. He is said to have written a वृत्ति on the Pūrvamīmāṁsā-sūtras also. However none of these has been universally accepted by the scholars in these fields. It is generally conceded that बोधायन was, historically speaking, the founder of Vaiṣṇava schools of philosophy.

Bodh-gayā
(‘Gayā [where बुद्ध attained] bodhi [or enlightenment]’)
------------------------------------------
Bodh-गया or बुद्ध-गया is one of the most holy places of पिल्ग्रिमगे for the Buddhists. It is here that the prince Siddhārtha गौतम attained ‘bodhi’ or spiritual enlightenment and became the बुद्ध.
This place is situated at a distance of ten kilometers (6.5 miles) from गया, the well-known place of Hindu पिल्ग्रिमगे. The chief attractions of this place are the peepul tree (Bodhi tree) (See BODHIVṚKṢA for details.) and the बुद्ध temple. The temple is 15 metres (50 ft.) square and the total height is 48 metres (160 ft.). There is a beautiful image of बुद्ध as also of Māyādevī (Buddha’s मोथेर्). Though tradition ascribes the building of this temple to अशोक (272-232 B. C.), the present one may have been built after the 7th century A.D. and altered several times. The existing one may have been a rebuilt structure of the 19th century.
An edict of अशोक is found in a cave nearby. The Buddhist Vihāra he is said to have built does not exist now, though its remnants are found here and there near the Bodhi tree.
Hiuen Tsang (7th cent. A. D.) had visited this place and has left a nice description of the same.

Bodhivṛkṣa
(‘the tree of bodhi or enlightenment’)
------------------------------------------
Prince Siddhārtha गौतम became गौतम the ‘Buddha’ (‘the Enlightened One’) after attaining ‘bodhi’ or enlightenment. The particular peepul tree(aśvattha-vṛkṣa—Ficus religiosa) under which he attained this bodhi, situated at गया (now known as बोध्-गया or बुद्ध गया), is called the बोधिवृक्ष. There is a stone slab under it, ‘Vajrāsana’ by name, sitting on which बुद्ध is said to have attained enlightenment.
The present tree may be about a hundred years old.
The original tree is believed to have sprung up spontaneously on the same day that बुद्ध was born. Hence it was called ‘sahajāta.’
The extant tree is an offshoot of the older ones, sprouted out of their roots over centuries. Apart from the emperor अशोक, king Śaśāṅka (7th cent. A. D.) is reported to have done the replanting. The latest one may have been done in 1876.
A branch of this tree was taken to Anūrādhapura (in Sri Lanka) and planted there by Saṅghamittā-therī (a Buddhist nun, daughter of emperor अशोक).
See also BODHGAYĀ.
